html:
The Pintupi are an Aboriginal people of the Western Desert, whose country lies around Lake Mackay and Lake Macdonald on the border of Western Australia and the Northern Territory. It is some of the driest and most remote land on the continent.

For centuries, including the years the map shows, they lived in small family groups that moved between rockholes and soaks, following rain. They stayed out of contact with settlers longer than almost anyone in Australia.

  • 1940s to 1960s: drought and government patrols drew or moved many Pintupi east to Haasts Bluff and Papunya.
  • 1971: Pintupi men at Papunya were among the founders of the Papunya Tula painting movement.
  • 1980s: groups moved back west to their own country and founded Kintore (Walungurru) and Kiwirrkurra.
  • 1984: the Pintupi Nine, a family who had never met settlers, walked out of the desert near Kiwirrkurra.

Their neighbours include the Luritja, Warlpiri and Kukatja. See Aboriginal Australian societies.
